DOI: 10.1039/d5ew00908a Michael Templeton is professor of public health engineering in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at Imperial College London and co-chair of the Imperial Global Development Lab Advisory Board. He holds the Oxfam and Water for People / Royal Academy of Engineering Research Chair in Global Sanitation Technology and is currently head of the environmental and water resource engineering section within the department. His extensive research and expertise focus on addressing engineering and public health challenges associated with water supply and sanitation. One area of his work explores innovative and sustainable sanitation solutions through vermifilter toilets, commonly known as "Tiger Worm Toilets," which use worms to break down human waste and reduce the need for frequent pit emptying. Tackling the global sanitation challenge Access to safe sanitation remains a significant global challenge. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), in 2022–2023, approximately 3.5 billion people (43% of the global population) lacked safely managed sanitation. This refers to access to a toilet or latrine where human waste is safely treated or disposed of. This year's U.N. World Toilet Day campaign, Safe toilets. Equal futures., highlights the importance of safe sanitation in supporting health and gender equality. However, improving access to toilets is only part of the challenge. Ensuring that sanitation systems are safe, affordable and sustainable is equally important. Traditional pit latrines can fill up over time, requiring waste to be removed and disposed of. This presents considerable health and safety risks, particularly in communities where professional waste management services are limited. An estimated 200 million latrines are manually emptied each year, with workers sometimes having to descend into pits to remove waste by hand, exposing themselves to harmful pathogens. An innovative solution: the Tiger Worm Toilet Originally conceived, designed and tested in 2010–2012 via a collaboration involving Imperial and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, the Tiger Worm Toilet offers an alternative approach to conventional sanitation systems. As the name implies, the technology uses tiger worms to break down human waste within latrines. The worms feed on organic matter, helping to reduce the accumulation of solid waste and hence slow the rate at which the pit fills. This process produces compost that is safer to handle than untreated fecal sludge in pit latrines, while also helping to treat the liquid within the waste. By reducing the volume of waste accumulating in the pit, Tiger Worm Toilets can significantly extend the time between emptying. This offers several practical benefits for communities, including reduced costs associated with emptying and waste disposal. By limiting the need for manual pit emptying, the technology could also help reduce the health risks faced by sanitation workers. A recent paper published by Templeton's research group showed that Tiger Worm Toilet user satisfaction remains high even after 10 years of use. The research is published in the journal Environmental Science: Water Research & Technology . More than just a toilet: creating equal futures The impact of inadequate sanitation extends far beyond public health. For example, without access to reliable toilet facilities in schools, women and girls face additional barriers to education, particularly during menstruation . In communities where suitable facilities are unavailable, girls may miss school or struggle to participate fully in their education. This highlights why sanitation must be recognized not simply as an engineering challenge, but as a wider societal issue. For Templeton, improving sanitation is therefore about more than engineering a better toilet. It is about addressing an issue that can shape people's everyday lives and opportunities, while ensuring that communities have access to infrastructure that supports their health, education and well-being.
